source_text: Ὥσπερ γὰρ οἱ τῶν ἔξωθεν ἄρχοντες οὐκ ἂν ἕλοιντο παρ' εὐτελέσι καὶ ταπεινοῖς καταχθῆναί ποτε, ἀλλ' ἐπιζητοῦσι λαμπρὰς οἰκίας ἐπισήμων ἀνδρῶν τινων, ὥστε μὴ τὴν τῶν ὑποδεχομένων αὐτοὺς εὐτέλειαν τῷ μεγέθει τῆς ἀξίας λυμήνασθαι· οὕτω καὶ οἱ ἀπόστολοι ἐποίουν· οὐ πρὸς τυχόντας κατήγοντο, ἀλλ' ὥσπερ ἐκεῖνοι οἰκίας λαμπρότητα, οὕτω τῆς ψυχῆς ἀρετὴν ἐπεζήτουν οὗτοι, καὶ μετὰ ἀκριβείας διερευνώμενοι τοὺς ἐπιτηδείους αὐτοῖς, πρὸς ἐκείνους κατήγοντο. Καὶ γὰρ καὶ νόμος παρὰ τοῦ Χριστοῦ τοῦτο κελεύων ἔκειτο. Εἰς ἣν γὰρ πόλιν, φησὶν, ἢ οἰκίαν εἰσέλθητε, ἐρωτήσατε τίς ἐν αὐτῇ ἄξιός ἐστι, κἀκεῖ μείνατε. Ὥστε ἄξιοι Παύλου ἦσαν οὗτοι· εἰ δὲ ἄξιοι Παύλου, τῶν ἀγγέλων ἦσαν ἄξιοι. Ἐγὼ τὸ δωμάτιον ἐκεῖνο, καὶ οὐρανὸν καὶ Ἐκκλησίαν θαῤῥῶν ἂν προσείποιμι. Ὅπου γὰρ Παῦλος ἦν, ἐκεῖ καὶ ὁ Χριστὸς ἦν. Εἰ δοκιμὴν ἐπιζητεῖτε, φησὶ, τοῦ ἐν ἐμοὶ λαλοῦντος Χριστοῦ; Ὅπου δὲ Χριστὸς ἦν, ἐκεῖ καὶ ἄγγελοι συνεχῶς ἐφοίτων. Οἱ δὲ καὶ πρὸ τούτου παρασχόντες ἑαυτοὺς ἀξίους τῆς τοῦ Παύλου θεραπείας, ἐννόησον τίνες ἐγένοντο, ἔτεσι δύο συνοικοῦντες αὐτῷ, καὶ σχῆμα, καὶ βάδισμα, καὶ βλέμμα, καὶ τρόπον στολῆς, καὶ εἰσόδους καὶ ἐξόδους, καὶ τἄλλα πάντα παρατηροῦντες. Ἐπὶ γὰρ τῶν ἁγίων οὐχὶ τὰ ῥήματα ταῦτα μόνον, οὐδὲ αἱ διδασκαλίαι καὶ αἱ παραινέσεις, ἀλλὰ καὶ ἡ λοιπὴ τοῦ βίου πᾶσα ἀναστροφὴ ἀρκοῦσα γένοιτ' ἂν τοῖς προσέχουσι διδασκαλία φιλοσοφίας. Ἐννόησον ἡλίκον ἦν ἰδεῖν Παῦλον, καὶ δειπνοποιούμενον, καὶ ἐπιτιμῶντα, καὶ παρακαλοῦντα, καὶ εὐχόμενον, καὶ δακρύοντα, ἐξιόντα καὶ εἰσιόντα. Εἰ γὰρ δεκατέσσαρας ἐπιστολὰς ἔχοντες μόνον, πανταχοῦ τῆς οἰκουμένης αὐτὰς περιφέρομεν, οἱ τὴν πηγὴν τῶν ἐπιστολῶν ἔχοντες, οἱ τὴν γλῶτταν τῆς οἰκουμένης, οἱ τὸ φῶς τῶν Ἐκκλησιῶν, οἱ τὸν θεμέλιον τῆς πίστεως, οἱ τὸν στῦλον καὶ τὸ ἑδραίωμα τῆς ἀληθείας, τίνες οὐκ ἂν ἐγένοντο ἀγγέλῳ τοιούτῳ συζῶντες; Εἰ γὰρ τὰ ἱμάτια αὐτοῦ δαίμοσιν ἦν φοβερὰ, καὶ τοσαύτην εἶχον ἰσχὺν, ἡ συνοίκησις αὐτοῦ πόσην οὐκ ἂν ἐπεσπάσατο Πνεύματος χάριν; Τὸ γὰρ τὴν κλίνην ὁρᾷν τὴν Παύλου, τὸ γὰρ τὴν στρωμνὴν, τὸ γὰρ τὰ ὑποδήματα, οὐκ ἂν ἤρκεσεν αὐτοῖς εἰς ὑπόθεσιν κατανύξεως διηνεκοῦς; Εἰ γὰρ οἱ δαίμονες ὁρῶντες αὐτοῦ τὰ ἱμάτια ἔφριττον, πολλῷ μᾶλλον οἱ πιστοὶ καὶ συζήσαντες αὐτῷ κατενύσσοντο βλέποντες αὐτά. Ἄξιον δὲ κἀκεῖνο ἐξετάσαι, τίνος ἕνεκεν, προσαγορεύων, τὴν Πρίσκιλλαν προτέθεικε τοῦ ἀνδρός. Οὐ γὰρ εἶπεν, Ἀσπάσασθε Ἀκύλαν καὶ Πρίσκιλλαν, ἀλλὰ, Πρίσκιλλαν καὶ Ἀκύλαν. Οὐδὲ γὰρ τοῦτο ἁπλῶς ἐποίησεν, ἀλλ' ἐμοὶ δοκεῖ πλείονα αὐτῇ συνειδέναι τοῦ ἀνδρὸς εὐλάβειαν. Καὶ ὅτι οὐ στοχασμὸς τὸ εἰρημένον, ἔξεστι καὶ ἀπὸ τῶν Πράξεων τοῦτο μαθεῖν. Τὸν γὰρ Ἀπολλὼ, ἄνδρα λόγιον ὄντα καὶ δυνατὸν ἐν ταῖς Γραφαῖς, καὶ τὸ βάπτισμα Ἰωάννου μόνον εἰδότα, αὕτη λαβοῦσα κατήχησε τὴν ὁδὸν τοῦ Θεοῦ, καὶ διδάσκαλον ἀπηρτισμένον ἐποίησεν. Οὐ γὰρ αἱ ἐπὶ τῶν ἀποστόλων γυναῖκες ταῦτα ἐμερίμνων, ἅπερ αἱ νῦν, ὅπως λαμπρὰ ἱμάτια περιβάλοιντο, καὶ ἐπιτρίμμασι καὶ ὑπογραφαῖς τὴν ὄψιν τὴν ἑαυτῶν καλλωπίσαιεν, καὶ τοὺς ἄνδρας τοὺς ἑαυτῶν ἐνάγχουσαι, τῆς γείτονος καὶ τῆς ὁμοτίμου πολυτελεστέραν ἀναγκάζουσαι πρίασθαι στολὴν, καὶ λευκοὺς ἡμιόνους, καὶ χρυσοπάστους χαλινοὺς, καὶ θεραπείαν εὐνούχων, καὶ πολὺν θεραπαινίδων ἐσμὸν, καὶ τὴν ἄλλην ἅπασαν τὴν καταγέλαστον φαντασίαν· ἀλλὰ ταῦτα πάντα ἀποσεισάμεναι, καὶ τὸν κοσμικὸν ἀποβαλοῦσαι τῦφον, ἓν μόνον ἐζήτουν, ὅπως κοινωνοὶ γένωνται τῶν ἀποστόλων, καὶ τῆς θήρας αὐτῶν μετάσχοιεν τῆς αὐτῆς.
thought_title: The apostles sought worthy souls, not fine houses
orientation: Chrysostom is explaining why Paul stayed with Priscilla and Aquila for two years, comparing the apostles' search for worthy souls to rulers' search for splendid houses.
pass_a_gloss: For just as the rulers of those outside would never choose to be lodged among cheap and humble people, but they seek splendid houses of certain distinguished men, so that the cheapness of those receiving them might not harm the greatness of their dignity; so also the apostles did; they were not lodged with random people, but just as those sought splendor of house, so these sought virtue of soul, and examining with exactness those suitable for them, they were lodged with those. For indeed also a law from Christ commanding this lay in place. For into whatever city, he says, or house you enter, ask who in it is worthy, and remain there. So these were worthy of Paul; and if worthy of Paul, they were worthy of the angels. I would confidently call that little room both heaven and Church. For where Paul was, there also Christ was. Do you seek proof, he says, of the Christ speaking in me? And where Christ was, there also angels continually came and went. And those who even before this provided themselves worthy of the service of Paul, consider what sort they became, living with him for two years, and observing his appearance, and walk, and glance, and manner of clothing, and entrances and exits, and all the other things. For in the case of the saints not only these words, nor the teachings and the exhortations, but also the whole remaining conduct of life would be sufficient for those paying attention as teaching of discipline. Consider how great a thing it was to see Paul, both making dinner, and rebuking, and exhorting, and praying, and weeping, going out and coming in. For if having only fourteen letters, we carry them around everywhere in the inhabited world, those having the fountain of the letters, those having the tongue of the inhabited world, those having the light of the Churches, those having the foundation of the faith, those having the pillar and the support of the truth, what sort would they not have become, living with such an angel? For if his garments were fearful to demons, and had so much power, how much grace of the Spirit would his dwelling together not have drawn down? For seeing the bed of Paul, for seeing the mattress, for seeing the sandals, would it not have sufficed for them as a basis of continual compunction? For if the demons seeing his garments shuddered, much more the faithful who also lived with him were pierced seeing them. And it is worth examining also that, for what reason, in greeting, he placed Priscilla before her husband. For he did not say, Greet Aquila and Priscilla, but, Priscilla and Aquila. For he did not do this simply, but it seems to me he was aware of more piety in her than in her husband. And that what is said is not a guess, it is possible to learn this also from the Acts. For Apollos, a man being learned and powerful in the Scriptures, and knowing only the baptism of John, this woman taking him instructed him in the way of God, and made him a fully equipped teacher. For the women in the time of the apostles did not busy themselves with these things, which the women now do, that they might put on splendid garments, and adorn their own face with cosmetics and paints, and choking their own husbands, forcing them to buy a more expensive robe than the neighbor woman and the woman of equal rank, and white mules, and gold-studded bridles, and a retinue of eunuchs, and a great swarm of maidservants, and all the other ridiculous display; but shaking off all these things, and casting away the worldly vanity, they sought one thing only, that they might become sharers of the apostles, and might share in their same hunt.

lemmas.gloss: to be lodged, brought down to stay
he has placed before, put first
to be aware of, know together

choices.why: Keeps the literal 'those outside' (οἱ ἔξωθεν) as a designation for secular society, preserving Chrysostom's insider/outsider framing
The verb means to be brought down and housed; 'lodged' keeps the sense of staying as a guest without modernizing to 'stay'
Literal rendering of the adjective λαμπράς as 'splendid' matches the contrast with the splendor of soul the apostles sought
Keeps the genitive construction literal and preserves the contrast between house-splendor and soul-virtue
The diminutive δωμάτιον is deliberately small; 'little room' preserves the affectionate diminutive force
The verb ἄγχω means to choke or strangle; Chrysostom uses it hyperbolically for wives pressuring husbands, and the literal force should be kept

pass_b_english: Just as the rulers of those outside would never choose to be lodged with cheap and humble people, but seek splendid houses belonging to men of note, so that the meanness of their hosts may not damage the greatness of their dignity, so the apostles did the same. They did not lodge with just anyone, but just as those rulers sought splendor of house, these sought virtue of soul, and after examining thoroughly who was suitable for them, they lodged with those people. For a law from Christ lay down this command. “Whatever city or house you enter,” he says, “ask who in it is worthy, and stay there” (Matthew 10:11). So these two were worthy of Paul; and if worthy of Paul, they were worthy of the angels. I would confidently call that little room both heaven and a church. For where Paul was, there Christ was. “If you seek proof,” he says, “of Christ speaking in me” (2 Corinthians 13:3). And where Christ was, there angels continually came and went. And think what sort of people they became who even before this had shown themselves worthy of serving Paul, living with him for two years and observing closely his bearing, his walk, his gaze, his manner of dress, his comings and goings, and everything else. For with the saints, not only their words, not only their teachings and exhortations, but the whole rest of their conduct is enough to be a teaching of discipline for those who pay attention. Think how great a thing it was to see Paul dining, rebuking, encouraging, praying, weeping, going out and coming in. If we, having only fourteen letters, carry them around everywhere in the world, what would those people not have become who had the source of the letters, the tongue of the world, the light of the churches, the foundation of the faith, the pillar and support of the truth, living with such an angel? For if his garments were fearsome to demons and had such power, how much grace of the Spirit would living with him not have drawn down? For seeing Paul’s bed, seeing his mattress, seeing his sandals—would that not have been enough for them as a ground for continual compunction? For if demons shuddered when they saw his garments, much more did the faithful who lived with him feel compunction when they saw them. It is worth examining also why, in greeting them, he placed Priscilla before her husband. For he did not say, “Greet Aquila and Priscilla,” but “Priscilla and Aquila.” He did not do this without reason, but it seems to me he was aware of greater piety in her than in her husband. And that this is not guesswork can be learned from the Acts. For Apollos, a man who was eloquent and powerful in the Scriptures and knew only the baptism of John—she took him and instructed him in the way of God, and made him a finished teacher. For the women in the apostles' time did not busy themselves with the things women busy themselves with now: how to put on splendid clothes, how to beautify their faces with ointments and paints, choking their husbands and forcing them to buy a more expensive robe than the neighbor’s wife or the woman of equal rank, and white mules, and gold-studded bridles, and a retinue of eunuchs, and a great swarm of maidservants, and all the rest of the ridiculous display. But casting off all these things and throwing away worldly vanity, they sought one thing only: to become partners with the apostles and share in their same hunt.

problems.why: 'ἐπὶ τῶν ἀποστόλων' means 'in the time of the apostles' or 'under the apostles,' not 'among the apostles.' These were not female apostles but women of that era.
problems.fix: the women in the apostles' time
problems.ruling: ἐπὶ τῶν ἀποστόλων means 'in the time of the apostles,' not 'among the apostles'; misleading.

edits.new: the women in the apostles' time

fixed: Changed 'the women among the apostles' to 'the women in the apostles' time' because the source 'αἱ ἐπὶ τῶν ἀποστόλων γυναῖκες' means women of that era, not female apostles.

problems.why: Middle-voice δειπνοποιέομαι means 'dining' or 'taking a meal', not 'preparing a meal' (active voice). Paul was their guest, not the cook.
problems.ruling: δειπνοποιούμενον (middle) is dining/taking a meal, not active 'preparing'; Paul seen as cook, not diner.

problems.why: The genitive is objective ('service/attendance to Paul', i.e. hosting and waiting on him), not subjective ('Paul's care' for them).
problems.ruling: ἀξίους τῆς θεραπείας: objective genitive—worthy to serve/host Paul—not subjective 'Paul's care' for them.

last_rejected.source_quote: νόμος παρὰ τοῦ Χριστοῦ τοῦτο κελεύων ἔκειτο
last_rejected.why: Subject is 'a law'; verb should be 'lay' not 'lay down'. 'Lay down' takes a direct object, but 'law' is the subject here.
last_rejected.fix: For a law from Christ lay down this command — For a law from Christ commanding this lay in place.
last_rejected.ruling: 'Lay down' correctly renders ἔκειτο (imperfect of κεῖμαι, 'was laid/established'); 'lay' alone would be ambiguous.

last_rejected.fix: Verify: Matthew 10:11 is correct for this wording.
last_rejected.ruling: Citation Matthew 10:11 matches source quote exactly; no error.

last_rejected.why: The Greek has 'the tongue of the world' (οἰκουμένης = inhabited world), but the English 'tongue of the world' is ambiguous — could mean 'language of the world.' The Greek means 'the voice/spokesman of the world.' 'Tongue' in older English can mean 'voice,' but modern readers may misunderstand.
last_rejected.ruling: γλῶτταν = tongue; normal range, not misleading in context.
